title: Dense-range perfect hash aggregate beyond perfect_ht_threshold
hypothesis: In q13 the inner HASH_GROUP_BY (count per integer key, 15.3M input rows, 1.5M groups) costs 3.08s of operator time, the largest operator in the plan. The integer group key has min/max stats whose range (about 2^21) is almost fully used by the groups. CanUsePerfectHashAggregate rejects it only because required_bits exceeds perfect_ht_threshold (default 12). I measured on the current build: `SET perfect_ht_threshold=24` switches it to PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY at 0.50s (6x less), and total query time drops from 1.08s to 0.95s under EXPLAIN ANALYZE. A direct-indexed array beats the radix-partitioned linear-probing HT when the key range is dense, because there is no hashing, no probing, no partitioning and no row materialisation.
plan: In src/execution/physical_plan/plan_aggregate.cpp, CanUsePerfectHashAggregate: keep the current threshold check as is. When perfect_hash_bits > threshold, allow a second 'dense' admission instead of returning false: (a) a single group column (or total bits) <= a fixed hard cap (for example 22 bits, about 4M slots); (b) the key range is dense, meaning the estimated number of groups (op.estimated_cardinality, or the child's estimated cardinality, whichever is the better group-count estimate; check what LogicalAggregate sets) is at least about 1/4 of 2^total_bits, so a mostly empty array is never allocated; (c) memory is bounded: threads (TaskScheduler::NumberOfThreads) * 2^bits * (payload tuple size estimate + 1 for group_is_set) must be <= a small fraction (for example 1/8) of BufferManager max memory, because PerfectAggregateHashTable allocates with make_unsafe_uniq_array (untracked, cannot spill; see src/execution/perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp:29-34). Keep the existing distinct and combine checks for both paths. Do not change the setting default. Add a short comment explaining the density and memory guards.
expected_gain: q13: inner aggregate 3.08s to about 0.5s of CPU; roughly 10-25% wall-clock on q13.
generality: Any GROUP BY on integer key(s) with min/max stats where the number of groups is close to the key range, such as grouping by a dense surrogate or primary key after a join, or by ids/dates stored as integers. Queries whose keys are sparse inside the range keep the normal hash aggregate thanks to the density guard. A wrong cardinality estimate could pick the perfect HT for a sparse range; that is still bounded by the bit cap and the memory guard, so it is slower but correct.
risk: Medium-low. The perfect HT path already exists and is tested. Risks are memory (it is untracked) and the serial finalize scan of 2^bits slots. Both are bounded by the cap and the memory fraction. Correctness for NULL keys is handled by the existing +2 range logic.

title: Profile RIGHT hash join probe on unique build key
hypothesis: HASH_JOIN RIGHT (build of 1.5M unique integer keys, probe of 14.8M rows) costs 1.8-2.0s of operator time, the next biggest cost after the aggregate. It is not yet investigated: possible causes are a probe with no perfect-hash join (the range is dense and unique), or the per-row found-match marking for the RIGHT outer join.
plan: Investigation first: read src/execution/operator/join/perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp and the conditions in physical_hash_join.cpp for when the perfect hash join is used (it may exclude RIGHT/OUTER joins or ranges above some size). File a concrete change after that.
generality: Outer joins against a dense unique-key dimension table.

title: Skip redundant found-match stores in RIGHT/FULL join probe
hypothesis: HASH_JOIN RIGHT costs 2.15s of operator CPU on q13, its second-biggest cost. The build side is 1.5M unique keys and 14.8M probe rows hit it, so each build row gets about 10 matches spread across 8 threads. In ScanStructure (src/execution/join_hashtable.cpp around line 1018-1027, inside the `PropagatesBuildSide(ht.join_type)` block), every match does an unconditional `Store<bool>(true, ptrs[idx] + ht.tuple_size)`. Each store is a write to a cache line that other cores hold in shared state. That forces an RFO/invalidation, so lines bounce between cores even though the flag is already true after the first match. The probe has just compared keys in that row, so the line is already in cache. Loading the flag first and storing only when it is false turns about 90% of these writes into cheap shared reads. The code already does this check-before-write in the RIGHT_SEMI/ANTI path (line 1145, `if (Load<bool>(ptr + ht.tuple_size))`), but the regular RIGHT/FULL path does not.
plan: In src/execution/join_hashtable.cpp, inside the matching loop that marks build-side found flags for PropagatesBuildSide join types (the loop at about line 1021 with `Store<bool>(true, ptrs[idx] + ht.tuple_size)`), change it to: `auto loc = ptrs[idx] + ht.tuple_size; if (!Load<bool>(loc)) { Store<bool>(true, loc); }`. Also apply the same guard to the store at about line 1168 (the non-equality-predicate branch of the RIGHT_SEMI/ANTI path). Nothing else changes. Semantics are the same because the only value ever written is true. Build and run bench on q13. Then run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to compare HASH_JOIN operator time (was 2.15s).
expected_gain: q13: HASH_JOIN operator time could drop substantially if coherence traffic dominates. Estimate 5-12% wall time on q13.
generality: Any RIGHT/FULL OUTER join (including LEFT joins flipped to RIGHT by the planner) where build rows match many probe rows across threads, such as fact-to-dimension outer joins. The cost is one extra predictable branch per match. A probe where every build row matches exactly once pays a tiny load+branch, which is negligible.
risk: Very low. It is a 3-line change with identical semantics, and the same pattern already exists in the same file.

title: Parallel/partitioned combine for perfect hash aggregate with large key range
hypothesis: E0001 (perfect hash aggregate up to 22 bits, guarded by density) cut q13's inner aggregate operator time from 3.14s to 0.53s, but wall time improved only 3.6%. PhysicalPerfectHashAggregate::Combine (src/execution/operator/aggregate/physical_perfecthash_aggregate.cpp:164-172) merges each thread's full 2^bits table into the global table under a single mutex. With 8 threads x 2M slots, that is a serial phase of about 16M slot merges, and the source then scans the table on one thread. So most of the CPU saved is lost to serialisation.
plan: Investigate first: profile E0001's variant (SET perfect_ht_threshold=22) and check whether the Finalize/Combine phase is the serial bottleneck. If it is, re-land E0001's CanUsePerfectHashAggregate heuristic and make the combine partitioned: split the slot range into ranges, and have each thread combine its own range from all local tables (for example via a Finalize event or a lock per range).
expected_gain: q13: maybe 10-15% if the serial combine is the remaining gap (operator CPU fell by about 2.6s)
generality: GROUP BY on dense integer keys with large ranges (ids, dates)
risk: Medium: changes the parallel structure of the operator. Needs the memory guard from E0001.

title: Parallel combine and parallel source for large perfect hash aggregate (re-land E0001)
hypothesis: E0001 cut q13's inner aggregate operator CPU from 3.14s to 0.53s, but wall time improved only 3.6%. I re-checked this round with SET perfect_ht_threshold=22: the PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY takes 0.45s, HASH_JOIN 1.59s and the scan about 2.4s, so about 4.4s of CPU in total, which is about 0.55s if spread over 8 threads. Wall time is still about 0.72-0.86s, the same as the radix-HA baseline (whose CPU of about 6.8s divided by 8 matches its wall time). So about 0.25s of the plan is serial. The code shows where. (1) PhysicalPerfectHashAggregate::Combine (physical_perfecthash_aggregate.cpp:164) takes one global mutex and calls PerfectAggregateHashTable::Combine (perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp:163), which walks all 2^bits slots of each local table. With 8 threads and 2M slots that is 16M slot visits, one table at a time. (2) PerfectHashAggregateState (source, line 178) has one shared ht_scan_position and no parallel source support. So the scan of 2M slots, FinalizeStates, and everything downstream (decompress projection, outer HASH_GROUP_BY over 1.5M rows) run on one thread. The radix HA baseline has a parallel source, so switching to the perfect HA made the downstream pipeline serial. That cancelled E0001's CPU win.
plan: (a) Re-land E0001's CanUsePerfectHashAggregate extension in src/execution/physical_plan/plan_aggregate.cpp (around line 127) with the same three guards: total bits at most max(threshold, 22); density, meaning estimated_cardinality >= 2^bits/4; and memory, meaning threads * 2^bits * (aligned state size + 1) <= max_memory/8. Keep the existing threshold path unchanged. (b) Add PerfectAggregateHashTable::CombineRange(other, begin, end, ArenaAllocator &alloc). It is Combine restricted to slots [begin,end), using a RowOperationsState built on the caller-provided arena. Moving other's aggregate_allocator into stored_allocators becomes a separate step done under the global lock. (c) In PerfectHashAggregateGlobalState, add a fixed array of stripe mutexes (for example 64 stripes, each a multiple of STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE slots) and an atomic start counter. Use the striped path only when total_groups >= 2^16. Small tables keep the existing single-lock path, so behaviour is unchanged for default-threshold queries. In Combine, each thread starts at stripe (atomic++ % S), visits every stripe in rotation, locks it and runs CombineRange into the global table with its own local ArenaAllocator. Afterwards, under the global lock, it pushes that arena and the local table's arena into stored_allocators. (d) Make the source parallel. Override MaxThreads in the global source state (ceil(total_groups / block) for large tables, 1 for small). Hand out blocks of slots (for example 2048*8) through an atomic counter. Add a per-thread LocalSourceState holding the current block range and its own ArenaAllocator for FinalizeStates. Add a PerfectAggregateHashTable::Scan overload that takes an end position. Check whether PhysicalPerfectHashAggregate already declares ParallelSource/GetLocalSourceState and set them as needed. Output order is not guaranteed for hash aggregates, so a parallel source is semantically fine.
expected_gain: q13: 10-20%. It removes about 0.15-0.25s of serial combine and source work while keeping E0001's 2.6s CPU saving.
generality: Any GROUP BY on dense integer keys with a large range (surrogate ids, dates, keys compressed to uinteger), for example per-customer and per-order counts or sums. Small perfect HAs (the default threshold of 12 bits or fewer) keep the exact old code path. Possible slowdowns: sparse key ranges that pass the density estimate wrongly. These are bounded by the density and memory guards.
risk: Medium. The arena allocator must never be shared between threads, so each combine and scan thread gets its own arena that is stored afterwards. Aggregates with destructors (Destroy loop) must still see each state exactly once. Stripe bounds must cover every slot. Results must be checked on aggregates beyond count (sum, min/max on strings, list) through hidden validation.

title: Perfect hash join for RIGHT joins on dense unique build keys
hypothesis: In the current best profile, HASH_JOIN RIGHT (build: 1.5M unique integer keys from the preserved side; probe: 14.8M rows) takes 1.70s of operator CPU. That is the second-largest cost after the 2.45s scan, while the perfect hash aggregate takes only 0.53s. The join currently goes through the generic hash probe: it hashes, follows chains, compares keys and marks the found flag in a random row. Two gates in PerfectHashJoinExecutor::CanDoPerfectHashJoin (src/execution/operator/join/perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp:66) exclude this join. Line 73 allows only INNER joins. Line 108 sets MAX_BUILD_SIZE=1048576, and the build range here is about 1.5M. A perfect probe is a range check plus a bitmap lookup per row and builds the build side as a dictionary vector. That should cut the join operator to about 0.3-0.4s CPU. The probe pipeline is fully parallel, so this saves roughly 1.3s/8, about 150ms wall.
plan:
1) CanDoPerfectHashJoin: also accept JoinType::RIGHT (build side preserved; PropagatesBuildSide). Keep INNER behaviour identical. Allow build_range above MAX_BUILD_SIZE up to 2^22 only if three guards hold. (a) Density: ht.Count()*4 >= build_range+1. (b) Memory: (build_range+1)*(sum of rhs_output column type sizes + 9) <= BufferManager max_memory/8. (c) No nested or VARCHAR columns on the RHS for the large-range path (or count string size conservatively). The existing duplicate check (Count > range) stays.
2) For RIGHT joins, PerfectHashJoinExecutor keeps two new arrays. The first is slot_to_row: data_ptr_t per slot. Fill it in FullScanHashTable from tuples_addresses and sel_build/sel_tuples, which are already computed there. The second is found: a uint8_t array per slot, zeroed. In ProbePerfectHashTable, for RIGHT, after FillSelectionVectorSwitchProbe set found[build_sel_vec[i]] = 1 for each match (a plain byte store; concurrent stores of the same value are benign). For a RIGHT join, probe rows without a match are dropped, which is already the slicing behaviour.
3) Before the full-outer scan, transfer the flags in physical_hash_join.cpp. Find where PrepareScanHT/the global source state sets up full_outer_chunk_count (around line 1291) and call a new PerfectHashJoinExecutor::PropagateFoundMatches() once, under the global source lock, before any ScanFullOuter. For each slot with found[idx], it stores true at slot_to_row[idx] + ht.tuple_size, the same location that JoinHashTable::ScanFullOuter (join_hashtable.cpp:1414) reads. Compare against match_propagation_value semantics. ScanFullOuter only iterates the data collection, and the perfect path skips the pointer-table Finalize, so the existing outer scan then works unchanged.
4) Verify with EXPLAIN that q13's join uses the perfect path. Check correctness with RIGHT/LEFT-swapped queries where some build keys are unmatched, a sparse key range, NULL build keys (has_null) and NULL probe keys, and compare count/sum against the same query forced through the regular join (for example with the key cast to varchar).
expected_gain: q13: join operator 1.70s down to about 0.4s CPU, roughly -15% to -25% wall
generality: Any outer join that preserves a dimension table with a dense integer primary key, which is common (customer/orders style LEFT JOIN, which the planner flips to RIGHT with the small side as build). Larger dense INNER joins (1M-4M range) also benefit from the raised cap. Possible slowdowns: a build that is dense but has a probe that mostly misses still pays the per-slot arrays (bounded by the guards).
risk: Medium. The found flag must reach the outer scan before it starts; a race or a missed transfer would give wrong outer rows. Raising the cap for INNER joins changes plans on other queries, but the density and memory guards bound it. Build columns that are strings live in the HT's data collection, and dictionary references to them stay valid because the HT stays alive.

title: SWAR first+last-byte candidate scan in FindStrInStr for short haystacks
hypothesis: In q13 the orders TABLE_SCAN with the NOT LIKE '%w1%w2%' filter is 2.40s of about 3.35s total operator CPU. Microbenchmarks at 8 threads, as scan operator CPU on orders: two integer columns only 0.41s; plus decoding o_comment with length(o_comment)>45 1.92s; NOT contains(o_comment,'qqqqqqq') with a rare first byte 2.23s; NOT contains 'eeeeeee' with a common first byte 2.44s; the actual q13 NOT LIKE 2.36s. At 1 thread the same scan is 2.09s, so the cost is per-row compute, not bandwidth. Matching therefore costs about 0.3-0.5s CPU on top of decoding. Even with a first byte that never occurs it costs about 0.3s, which is the fixed cost per string of calling memchr. FindStrInStr (src/function/scalar/string/contains.cpp:76) calls memchr for needle[0], then Contains<> calls memchr again for every candidate position. On short strings (about 50 bytes) with common first bytes, that means several libc calls per string, each with setup and branch overhead. A branch-light candidate filter would mostly remove the matcher cost: compare 8 (SWAR) or 16 (SSE2) positions at once against needle[0] at offset i and against needle[n-1] at offset i+n-1, AND the two masks, and verify only the surviving candidates with memcmp (Muła's generic SIMD strstr).
plan: In src/function/scalar/string/contains.cpp, add a fast path inside FindStrInStr(const unsigned char*, idx_t, const unsigned char*, idx_t), used when needle_size >= 2 and haystack_size >= needle_size - 1 + 8. Set first = broadcast(needle[0]) and last = broadcast(needle[n-1]). For i in steps of 8 while i + n - 1 + 8 <= haystack_size: A = Load<uint64_t>(h+i) ^ first; B = Load<uint64_t>(h+i+n-1) ^ last; take the zero-byte mask of (A|B) with the classic haszero ((x - 0x0101..) & ~x & 0x8080..). It can give false positives only above a true zero byte, and memcmp catches those. For each set bit, from low to high: pos = i + ctz(mask)/8; if memcmp(h+pos+1, needle+1, n-2) == 0, return pos (n==2 needs no memcmp). Positions must be visited in ascending order so the leftmost match is returned, because LikeMatcher::Match depends on the leftmost offset. After the loop, hand the remaining tail [i, end) to the existing memchr/Contains<> code with base_offset=i, or to a plain scalar loop. Every load must stay inside [haystack, haystack+haystack_size), with no over-read. Optionally use SSE2 for 16-byte blocks under #ifdef __SSE2__ with _mm_movemask_epi8, keeping the SWAR path as the portable fallback. Little-endian only for ctz bit order: on big-endian, use the existing path (#if on __BYTE_ORDER__). Keep the semantics identical: return the offset of the first match or INVALID_INDEX. Test against the old implementation on random strings, needles of length 1-20, matches at the start, at the end, overlapping and repeated-prefix cases, plus contains/strpos/LIKE/ILIKE queries.
expected_gain: q13: about 0.2-0.35s of the roughly 0.45s matcher CPU (of 3.35s total), so -5 to -10% wall. Any LIKE '%x%', contains, strpos or instr filter on string columns gets faster.
generality: Every substring search: LIKE with % segments, contains(), position/strpos/instr, NOT LIKE, ILIKE after lowercasing if it routes here. No query shape should get slower, except possibly very long haystacks with a rare first byte, where glibc's AVX2 memchr would beat 8-byte SWAR. The SSE2 variant or a fallback to memchr when haystack_size > 256 removes that case.
risk: Low to medium. It is a pure function with exact semantics, but over-reads and returning the leftmost match must be right. It is easy to unit-test against the old code.

title: Remove cancelling decompress/compress projection pair above joins
hypothesis: In the q13 plan, above the RIGHT HASH_JOIN, a PROJECTION applies __internal_decompress_integral_bigint(#1) (0.18s CPU on 15.3M rows, dictionary vectors from the perfect hash join). Right above it, another PROJECTION applies __internal_compress_integral_uinteger(#1) with the same offset for the aggregate's group key. The pair is an identity on the compressed value (the uinteger stays in range, since it was produced by the same compress), so it is wasted work, and it flattens dictionary vectors.
plan: Investigate where compress projections are added (grep for __internal_compress_integral in src/optimizer/compressed_materialization*.cpp). Add a rule that recognises compress_T(decompress_S(x, c), c) with the same constant offset where the compressed type T equals the input type of x, and replace it with x. That holds when the intermediate type is wider and the stats prove the range. Apply it either in CompressedMaterialization or as a peephole when two adjacent projections are merged.
expected_gain: q13: about 0.18s CPU of 3.35s, so -3 to -5%
generality: Any plan where compressed materialization wraps consecutive operators (join then aggregate) on the same integer key.
risk: Medium. The optimizer has to prove the offsets and types match. The gain is near the noise floor alone.

title: Reuse a per-scan-state string heap for FSST decoded strings
hypothesis: In q13 the orders TABLE_SCAN costs 2.37s of the roughly 3.3s operator CPU. Round 5 microbenchmarks put o_comment decode at about 1.5s, about 100ns per string, which is far above the FSST decoder's speed of about 1 cycle per byte, and the overhead was never explained. In FSSTStorage::StringScanPartial<false> (src/storage/compression/fsst.cpp:696-701), every non-inlined string goes through FSSTPrimitives::DecompressValue (src/include/duckdb/common/fsst.hpp:36). That calls VectorStringBuffer::AllocateShrinkableBuffer(len*8) on the result vector's string heap. The scan vector's auxiliary is dropped on every chunk reset, so StringVector::GetStringBuffer (vector.cpp:2218) makes a fresh VectorStringBuffer whose ArenaAllocator starts at 2KB. ArenaAllocator::AllocateNewBlock (arena_allocator.cpp:63) doubles the block size, so each 2048-row vector of ~50-byte strings (about 100KB, plus len*8 headroom) does about 7 mallocs of 4KB to 256KB. It also wastes the leftover space of every old block. The larger blocks come from glibc malloc (no jemalloc is loaded), which serves them as fresh, often mmapped pages, so the scan page-faults and touches cold memory on every vector. Keeping one heap per scan state and reusing it when nobody else holds a reference fixes this: after warm-up, ArenaAllocator::Reset (arena_allocator.cpp:136) keeps the largest head block, so later vectors do zero mallocs into hot, already-mapped memory.
plan:
In src/storage/compression/fsst.cpp:
1) Add `buffer_ptr<VectorStringBuffer> cached_string_buffer;` to FSSTScanState.
2) In StringScanPartial, in the non-FSST-vector branch (line 696), before calling StringVector::GetStringBuffer, check three conditions: result_offset == 0, result has no auxiliary yet, and the vector type is FLAT. If they all hold:
   - If cached_string_buffer exists and cached_string_buffer.use_count() == 1, meaning no downstream vector or chunk still references it, reset its heap. Add a small `void Reset()` to StringHeap that calls allocator.Reset(), and expose it on VectorStringBuffer.
   - Otherwise create a new one, with make_buffer<VectorStringBuffer>() or with the result buffer's allocator, the same way GetStringBuffer does.
   - Then set result's auxiliary to cached_string_buffer. Use the existing setter if there is one (grep for SetAuxiliary in vector.hpp); otherwise use StringVector::AddBuffer semantics, or assign `result.auxiliary` through a friend or accessor.
   - Then proceed as before.
   Do not touch the case where result_offset > 0 (a scan continuing in the same vector across segments): keep the existing buffer there.
3) Optionally, reserve once per call to avoid the doubling chain on first use: sum the compressed lengths for this call, multiply by 8, and pre-grow the arena with a single Allocate and ShrinkHead, so there is one block per vector instead of seven.
Correctness: use_count()==1 guarantees nothing else holds the strings. Operators that keep strings (hash tables, sorts, Vector::Reference copies) either hold a reference to the auxiliary, which raises use_count so we don't reuse, or copy the strings into their own heaps. Check that DataChunk/Vector Reference and Slice share the auxiliary buffer_ptr rather than copying raw pointers. If any path copies string_t without the auxiliary, the reuse is unsafe there; check this with grep on `auxiliary` in vector.cpp.
Validate with:
- the q13 bench
- SELECT of the full o_comment column with ORDER BY/LIMIT, and string_agg over a group by
- a hash join with string payload, which must keep its strings after the scan advances
- CREATE TABLE AS SELECT of the column, compared by hash against the original
Compare all of these with checksums such as sum(hash(o_comment)) under the old and new builds.
expected_gain: q13: if the allocation and page-fault overhead is a large part of the 1.5s decode, about -10 to -20% wall (scan is about 70% of CPU). At minimum it saves the 7 mallocs per vector, so likely at least -5%.
generality: Every scan of an FSST-compressed VARCHAR column with non-inlined strings, which covers most string columns in persistent DuckDB databases: comments, names, addresses. It helps filters, projections and string aggregations. Nothing should get slower: when the buffer is still referenced downstream, it falls back to a fresh buffer exactly as today. The only cost is one cached heap per scan state, at most about 16MB if one vector held huge strings.
risk: Medium. The main risk is a use-after-free if some downstream path keeps string_t pointers without holding the vector's auxiliary buffer_ptr. The use_count check covers every holder that keeps a reference. Hidden-query correctness checks will catch the rest. Memory held per scan thread is bounded by the largest vector's decoded size.
